 country drew the attention of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
 Culture and accordingly the Committee decided to take up the various aspects of  'Development of Airport Sector with
 special emphasis on new modern airports' for study and examination.
 
2.         The Committee requested the Ministry of Civil Aviation to furnish a detailed background note on the subject for
 consideration of the Committee.  The Committee also held the oral evidence of the representatives of Ministry of Civil
 Aviation and Airports Authority of India on the 8 th November and 28 th December 2004 and 6 th June and 29 th June
 2005.  The Committee also sought replies to the queries on the subject during the oral evidence of the Secretary and
 other representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation during the examination of Demands for Grants 2005-06 of the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The various aspects of the subject discussed by the Committee and the Committee's
 observations thereon have been brought out in the succeeding paragraphs of the report.
MODERNISATION AND RESTRUCTURING OF DELHI AND MUMBAI AIRPORTS
 
3.         As per their plans for developmental process of airports, the Ministry of Civil Aviation had taken steps to
 modernize and restructure Delhi and Mumbai airports through Joint Venture route.  The Ministry of Civil Aviation
 provided the following brief consisting of the details of various steps the Government took towards restructuring and
 modernization of Delhi and Mumbai airports:-
 
The Cabinet in its meeting held on 11 th September 2003 accorded its approval for the restructuring of Delhi and
 Mumbai airports by adopting the Joint-Venture route.
 
The AAI Amendment Bill introduced in the Parliament (Budget Session 2003) was passed by the Parliament in
 the Monsoon Session of June 2003.  The Amendment Bill authorizes AAI to transfer the operations and
 management of its existing airports by way of long-term lease to private players.  The Bill inter alia provides for
 exclusion of private airports (like BIAL) from the ambit of AAI Act, excepting security and ATC functions,
 which will continue to be discharged by AAI.  The Bill also authorizes AAI to change Advance Development
 Fee (ADF) for the development/upgradation of existing airports and for the setting up of Greenfield airports.  In
 addition, the Bill also seeks to prevent and remove encroachments of airport land.  The provisions of Airports
 Authority of India (Amendment) Act 2003 became effective w.e.f. 1 st July 2004, as per Gazette Notification
 dated 1st July 2004. 
 
The Cabinet constituted an Empowered Group of Ministers (EGOM) to take up decisions on various issues
 connected with the restructuring of Mumbai and Delhi airports. In this connection the Cabinet also decided to
 constitute an Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG) to assist EGOM.  The IMG was accordingly constituted by Ministry
 of Civil Aviation during October 2003 under the Chairmanship of Additional Secretary & Financial Advisor of
 MCA and other Members from the MCA, MoF, Department of Disinvestment and Ministry of Law, Justice &
 Company Affairs and AAI.
 
To assist Ministry of Civil Aviation (MOCA)/Airports Authority of India (AAI) in the restructuring process, AAI
 invited technical & financial bids for the appointment of Financial Consultants.  M/s. ABN AMRO were selected
 as Financial Consultants and they started the work in January 2004.
 
After obtaining the approval of EGOM, Registration of Expressions of Interest were solicited from interested
 parties to acquire 74% equity state in the JVC and the complete documentation, in this regard, was uploaded in
 the websites of AAI and MCA on 17.02.2004.  The last date for submission of EOI was 04.06.2004.
 
Subsequent to formation of the new Government, the Hon'ble Minister of State for Civil Aviation discussed in

90th Report of the Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture

 detail few critical issues relating to the Transaction including the quantum of foreign direct investments.  In order
 to address these critical issues, the last date of submission of Expression of Interest was extended to 20 th July
 2004.
 
The Cabinet in its meeting held on 15 th June 2004 reconstituted the EGOM under the Chairmanship of Defence
 Minister to take the Transaction forward.
 
The reconstituted EGOM has, inter-alia, approved the 49% cap of FDI, restriction of equity participation by
 Indian Scheduled Airlines upto 10% increasing the deputation period of employees in the JVCs from 2 to 3 years
 and also decided to give weightage to bidders who will induct more number of employees over and above the
 mandatory induction of 40% net.
 
The EGOM also approved the appointment of M/s. Airplan, Australia as the Global Technical Advisor and M/s.
 Amarchand & Mangaldas Suresh A. Shroff as legal Consultant.
 
Ten entities have lodged their EOIs by 20th July 2004 (i.e. last date of the receipt of EOIs).  Evaluation of EOIs is
 on hand.  
 
Subsequent to the approval of the Board of AAI, M/s. Thakur, Vaidyanath Aiyar & Co. has been appointed an
 Accounting and Tax Advisor for the Transaction and they have since started their assignment.
 
4.         The Committee desired to know from Ministry of Civil Aviation as to what was meant by modernization of
 these airports.  In response, the Committee was informed by Ministry that the modernization of these airports would
 mean the attainment/achievement of the key strategic objectives of the Government of India as envisaged for the
 transaction, which are as under:
 
(i)                  World Class development and expansion - Under this objective, a world-class phased
 development/expansion is contemplated through timely provision of high quality airport infrastructure
 on both airside and landside to meet growing traffic demands.
 
(ii)                World Class airport management - Under this objective, a world class airport management team and
 systems is contemplated by selection of successful bidders with suitable operational experience,
 managerial and financial capability, financial commitment and the commitment to provide quality
 airport service.
 
5.         In addition to the key Transaction objectives, other Transaction objectives include:
·        Timely completion and certainty of closure, with minimal residual risks;
·        Smooth transition of operations, under concession agreements;
·        Appropriate regulation-achieving economic regulation of aeronautical assets that is fair, commercially and
 economically appropriate,  transparent, predictable, consistent and stable while protecting the interest of
 users and ensuring that the Airports are operated in accordance with world standards;
 
·        Fair and equitable treatment of AAI employees, including preservation of accrued entitlement; and
 
·
        Diversity of ownership between Delhi and Mumbai airports, to enhance competition, encourage innovation
 and allow competitive benchmarking.

6.         During the course of oral evidence of the Meeting held on 8 th November 2004, the Secretary, Ministry of Civil
 Aviation while giving details of development of airport sector in the country informed the Committee as under:-
           
"We have estimated that Delhi and Mumbai Airports would require an investment of roughly
 around Rs.10,000/- to Rs.20,000/- crore .  There are 23 smaller airports which would require an
 investment of around Rs.5000/- each.  The Greenfield airports would requirement of Rs.3,596 crore."
 
7.         The Committee was surprised to note the statement of the Secretary that as per their estimates, Delhi and
 Mumbai airports would require an investment of Rs.10,000 to Rs.20,000 crore.  The Committee, therefore, desired to
 know the budget cost estimates for modernization and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai airports.  The Ministry of
 Civil Aviation vide their O.M. No.H-11013/3/2004-AAI dated 12th January 2005 informed the Committee that so far as
 Mumbai airport was concerned, based on the study carried out by the Financial Consultant appointed by Airports
 Authority of India, the annual aircraft movement is expected to grow up from 151,000 movements in 2004 to 500,000
 movements in 2024 and correspondingly the annual passenger movement is expected to go up from 14 million in 2004
 to 52 million in 2024.  This increase in traffic will call for airfield capacity enhancement as also enhancement in
 terminal capacity.  As per the staged development plan worked out by M/s. Airplan Limited, Australia (Global
 Technical Adviser appointed by AAI), the budget cost estimates in respect of Mumbai Airport is of the order of
 Rs.6300 crore for the period from 2005-2019.
 
8.         As regards Delhi Airport, based on the study carried out by the Financial Consultant appointed by Airports
 Authority of India, the annual aircraft  movement is expected to grow up from 117,000 movements in 2004 to 402,000
 movements in 2024 and correspondingly the annual passenger movement is expected to go up from 11.2 million in
 2004 to 42.8 million in 2024.  This increase in traffic will call for airfield capacity enhancement as also enhancement in
 terminal capacity.  As per the staged development plan worked out by M/s. Airplan Limited, Australia [Global
 Technical Adviser appointed by Airports Authority of India], the Budget cost estimates in respect of Delhi Airport is of
 the order of Rs.6500 crore for the period from 2005-2024.
 
9.         The Ministry of Civil Aviation further informed that while the above estimates have been made by the Global
 Technical Adviser (which does not include costs on account of relocation of some existing assets and for removal of
 encroachments), as per the transaction process, the prospective bidders are required to submit their development plans
 taking into account the mandatory facilities to be created in the short-term, which would be prescribed by Airports
 Authority of India/Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The successful bidders will have to submit their master plan within one
 year of their selection, which will be in conformity with the development plans submitted alongwith their bids. 
 Accordingly, the cost estimates as indicated above may undergo appropriate/suitable changes (upward or downward) in
 the light of development plans/master plan of the successful bidders.

 Approx. Rs.6400 crore need to be incurred in the next 20 years.  Similarly, Delhi is expected to handle 428 million
 passengers by 2024 and investment of approx. Rs.8720 crore is required in the next 20 years.

th June 2005 the
 Committee expressed surprise at the statement made by the Secretary regarding the quantum of investment estimated
 for development of Delhi and Mumbai airports.  The Secretary, while clarifying the statement made by him on 8 th

 Mumbai airports, stated as under:-
 
"I said that tentatively the estimated cost of modernization and development of these airports would be
 around ten to twenty thousand crore.  You had very rightly pointed out that the range was quite wide and
 that it showed that full examination of the question had not taken place.  Since then, there have been a
 number of things that have happened.  We had appointed a global technical advisor, an Australian
 company, which has been working as consultant and advisor to a number of international airports,
 including Hong Kong etc., in Asia.   We tasked them to draw up an initial development plan for Delhi
 and Mumbai, both.  They have now come up with an initial development plan.  I would hasten to add
 here that this is not the final plan.  The final plan will be prepared by the concessionaire who wins the
 bid.  This is an initial development plan prepared by our technical advisers and according to this the
 investment in Delhi Airport is to be done in four stages.  The first stage would commence now. As soon
 as the bidding process is completed by the concession agreements, it will go up to year 2009.  This
 figure of 2009, we have determined keeping in view the hosting by Delhi of the Commonwealth Games
 which are going to be held in 2010.  The second phase would be between 2010 and 2014 and the third
 phase would be between 2015 and 2019.  The fourth phase would be between 2020 and 2024.  By 2024,

 revenue sharing will be decided.  When the bids come in, each of the bidders will submit his own plan for development
 of these airports.  The bidder can configure the development plan and find a better way of providing all the facilities.  It

 airports.  The Committee notes that due to problems of capacity and locational constraints, the new airports are being

68.       The Committee enquired from the Ministry of Civil Aviation about the conditions stipulated while permitting
 private airlines to operate with regard to making them CAT-III B compliant.  In response, the Committee has been
 informed that as of now, there is no legal requirement in the Aircraft Rules and Civil Aviation Requirements that makes
 it mandatory for private airlines to train their pilots on ILS CAT- III B System.  However, various airlines have been
 coordinated from time to time to train their pilots for using the ILS CAT-III System in order to improve their
 operational efficiency during poor visibility conditions. 
 
69.       The Committee enquired about the details of the Training facilities available with the private airlines and
 monitoring mechanism available with the DGCA, the Ministry of Civil Aviation informed the Committee that the
 private airlines have their own arrangements for training both in ground courses as well as on simulator.  Jet Airways
 have their training establishments at Mumbai excepting simulator training for ATR which is done at Bangkok. 
 Similarly, Sahara Airlines has arrangements with Alteon, U.K. for both ground and simulator training on Boeing type
 aircraft and at CAE Facility, Spain for CRJ-200 aircraft.  Air Deccan carries out both ground and simulator training for
 their pilots on Airbus-320 and ATR aircraft at the Aircraft Manufacturer’s Facility at Toulouse, France.  These training
 facilities are initially approved by the DGCA based on their quality and capacity of training and on the basis of the
 approval of the state in which these establishments are located.  The training establishments in India are also
 periodically inspected by DGCA officers in the course of Safety Audits, Main Base Inspections and other surveillance
 activities.
 
70.       The Committee is constrained to note that on the one hand, the Government has cited resource crunch as the
 prime reason for inviting private sector participation in modernization of airports while on the other hand, the costly
 technologies installed at the airports after making huge investments remain idle due to want of trained personnel.  Also
 while the current policy of the Government aims at allowing more and more airlines to operate in the country, it has not
 made it obligatory for them to utilize the modern facilities installed at the airports with huge investments for the
 convenience of the passengers.  The Committee is surprised to note that the three private airlines i.e. Jet Airways,
 Sahara Airlines and Air Deccan have not trained any of their pilots for CAT-III operations and there is no legal
 requirement in the Aircraft Rules and Civil Aviation requirements to make it mandatory for private airlines to train their
 pilots on ILS CAT-III System.  The Committee is also not satisfied with the progress achieved with respect to the
 training of the pilots by the National Carriers viz. Indian Airlines and Air India, for utilizing the CAT-III System.  The
 Committee recommends that in order to improve the operational efficiency during the extreme foggy conditions, the
 Ministry should amend 'Aircraft Rules' to incorporate a provision for making training of pilots compulsory by the
 private airlines on CAT-III System so that the investment made by the Government on the installation of the system
 through the tax payers' money is not underutilized.  The Committee hopes that the national carriers and the private

71.       The Committee also sought details regarding the development on non-metro airports in the country.  The
 Ministry of Civil Aviation submitted a brief on the subject which stated that a concept paper was circulated by Ministry
 of Civil Aviation in August 2002 for city side development of Non-Metro Airports.  The proposal envisaged that entire
 operational area i.e. runway, taxiway, apron, communication & navigation aids, Air Traffic Management will remain
 with Airports Authority of India.  The expenditure incurred thereon and the revenue earned thereof shall be that of
 Airports Authority of India.  The city side of the airports i.e. non-operational areas which include the terminal building,
 car park, entire area outside the operational boundary wall will only be taken up for development.  The security and
 safety of viable Non-Metro Airports will continue with Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), Government of
 India and Airports Authority of India and will be maintained as per Government of India guidelines.

 Institution/State Government for city side development of viable Non-Metro Airports.

Report
            India is one of the oldest civilizations in the world and its historical heritage and cultural glory has been the
 subject of interest of the entire humanity.  In a country like India, endowed with both tangible and intangible heritage of
 an immense cultural and artistic value, which also has a multi-religious cultural fabric, archaeology assumes a position
 of crucial importance.
2.         Keeping in view the importance of archaeology, the Archaeological Survey of India was established in the year
 1861 with the primary object of surveying and recording the archaeological monuments in India.  It has a long colonial
 history and its mandate has evolved at a very slow pace spread over centuries.  For the first time in the year 1880, an
 organized attempt was made to preserve the monuments from decay by appointing Mr. H.H. Cole as a curator of
 monuments, which also coincided, with the recognition of the fact that the preservation of the monument was the
 permanent responsibility of the State.  In 1899, the Archaeological Survey of India was administratively divided into
 five circles for the preservation, conservation, archaeological exploration and excavation on a permanent basis and with
 well defined polices.  With the advent of Lord Curzon as Viceroy, the Archaeological Survey of India was placed on a
 formal footing during the first decade of the 20
th century.  He appointed Mr. John Marshal as the Director General of
 Archaeological Survey of India, who undertook great excavation at Taxila, Sanchi, Sarnath etc. The concept of
 archaeological conservation of ancient monuments was added during the time of John Marshall.  Hundreds of
 monuments/sites were declared as protected monuments under the purview of the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act
 1904.  In 1944, Dr. R.E.M. Wheeler was appointed Director General of Archaeological Survey of India.  During his
 tenure he incorporated modern methods for carrying archaeological excavations and trained the staff of the Survey in
 excavations at Taxila, Arikamedu and Harappa.  Having indepth understanding and involvement he revolutionized the
 concept of archaeological excavation by introducing importance of stratigraphy.  Wheeler also started Horticulture
 Branch in Archaeological Survey of India to develop suitable gardens to create pollution free ambiance around
 monuments.  Thus, prior to independence a sound foundation was laid for the Archaeological Survey of India. 
CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS IN THE POST INDEPENDENCE PERIOD:
3.         With the promulgation of the Constitution of India from 26
th January 1950, ‘archaeology’ has been made a
 Concurrent subject under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, which reads :
List I (Union List), item 67: ancient and historical monuments and records, and archaeological sites and remains
 declared by or under law by Parliament to be of national importance.
List II (State List), item 12: libraries, museums and other similar institutions controlled or financed by the State; ancient
 and historical monuments and records other than those declared by or under law made by Parliament to be of national
 importance.
List III (Concurrent List), item 40: archaeological sites and remains other than those declared by or under law made by

91stReport of Committee On Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/91streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:19]
 Parliament to be of national importance.
4.         In fulfillment of the provisions of the Constitution, Parliament passed the “Ancient and Historical Monuments
 and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act” in 1951 by which all the monuments previously protected under the
 Ancient Monuments Preservation Act 1904 were re-declared to be of national importance.  In 1953, after the merger of
 the princely states with the rest of India, the Archaeological Survey of India took the additional responsibility of upkeep
 of the monuments in princely states.
5.         Currently, the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 and Rules, 1959 and the
 Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972 and Rules, 1973 are operational and empowers the Archaeological Survey of
 India in its functioning.  
PRESENT MANDATE OF THE ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
6.         The Archaeological Survey of India is the premier organization so far as the archaeological research, study,
 excavation of archaeological sites, conservation/preservation of centrally protected monuments, maintenance of site
 museums and overall regulation of antiquities and art objects are concerned. As an apex body in the field of
 archaeology, the functions of Archaeological Survey of India are very broad and varied which may be classified as
 under :-
Conservation and preservation of monuments/sites and remains;
Archaeological explorations and excavations;
Preservation of monuments and antiquarian remains;
Architectural survey of monuments;
Epigraphical and numismatic studies;
Setting up of the Site Museums;
Training in archaeology;
Archaeologial publications;
Archaeological expeditions abroad;
Implementation of Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972; and
Horticulture operation around ancient monuments and sites.
7.         Since the functions of Archaeological Survey of India are very broad and varied and India is endowed with
 tremendous historical and cultural heritage, the Committee decided to study the functioning of Archaeological Survey
 of India.  In order to get wider views on the subject, the Committee decided to elicit the views of some independent
 experts in the field of archaeology.  Accordingly, the Committee heard the views of Shri S.S. Biswas, former Director
 General, National Museum and Shri Jagatpati Joshi, former Director General, Archaeological Survey of India on the
 17
th September and 1st October 2004 respectively.   On the basis of the information provided by these two independent
 experts and other documents provided to the Committee by the Ministry of Culture, the Committee took the oral
 evidence of the Secretary, Ministry of Culture and the representatives of Archaeological Survey of India on the 29
th
 November and 27th December 2004 and the 20th June 2005 to get an indepth insight into the functioning of
 Archaeological Survey of India.
MONUMMENTS/SITES UNDER PROTECTION OF ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
8.         Archaeological Survey of India protects and maintains 3663 monuments/sites in total and also declared those
 monuments as of national importance.  All the monuments/sites protected by the Archaeological Survey of India are
 being conserved/preserved on need based requirement.  As regards classification of monuments into different
 categories, the ASI has drawn long term programme to protect all 3663 monuments/sites which are of historical,
 architectural and aesthetic value.  Classification of monuments is an ongoing process and depends upon the
 requirements and feasibility of management, protection of monuments/sites.  In view of the nature of importance,
 urgency for structural conservation, preservation and chemical preservation including environmental development and
 providing essential tourist facilities in all these monuments, the ASI has categorised the monuments as under: -
Category of Monuments
                             No. of Monuments
1. Group A                                                       18 (which are inscribed
on the World Heritage List of UNESCO and are ticketed)
2. Group B                                                      108  (These are other
ticketed monuments/sites)    
3. Group C                   3537 (Unticketed
monuments/sites)
However, the Ministry made it clear that the above categorization is not a formal one, but for the convenience sake the

91stReport of Committee On Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/91streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:19]
 monuments have been categorized. 
9.         The Committee notes that the ASI has drawn long-term programme to protect all 3663 monuments/sites of
 national importance out of which 3537 monuments/sites are unticketed.  These monuments have also been classified
 into three categories viz. Group A, B and C for convenience.    The Committee is however aware that there are many
 sites/monuments under the protection/maintenance of Archaeological Survey of India which are located in interior
 areas of various States but are lying unattended. Therefore, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Culture should
 equally treat the revenue earning and not-earning sites and efforts should be made for integrated infrastructure
 development and conservation/preservation of all monuments/sites with encompassing facilities for tourists, so as to
 give a major fillip to cultural tourism in the country as well as attracting overseas visitors.                   
ORGANISATIONAL SET UP AND THE POST OF DIRECTOR GENERAL OF THE ARCHAEOLOGICAL
 SURVEY OF INDIA
10.       At present the Archaeological Survey of India is functioning as an attached office under the Ministry of Culture,
 which is headed by the Union Minister for Culture.  The Ministry of Culture has a Secretary level officer, who looks
 after various attached and subordinate office in the Ministry.  Being an attached office, the Archaeological Survey of
 India has its own head designated as Director General.  The Director General, in turn, is assisted by an Additional
 Director General, a Joint Director General and a group of Directors.  At present there are 10 Directors assisting the
 Director General in performing duties.  For administrative convenience and research purposes, the Archaeological
 Survey of India  is divided into 21 Circles headed by a Superintending Archaeologist, who is further assisted by Deputy
 Superintending Archaeologist., Deputy S.A.E., A.S.A., A.S.A.E., Ass & C.As.  There are 6 Excavation Branches, on
 Prehistory Branch, one Building Survey Project, two Temple Survey Projects, two Epigraphy Branches and one
 Science Branch functioning in the Archaeological Survey of India on different field and research project.
11.       The Archaeological Survey of India is headed by a Director General.  Some of the important functions and
 responsibilities of the Director General, Archaeological Survey of India are as under:
To function as the head of the Archaeological Survey of India which is primarily engaged on (a) basic research in
 various disciplines of archaeology, including (i)archaeological excavations and explorations (ii) protection of
 monuments/sites of national importance, their proper maintenance and upkeep and carrying of archaeological
 conservation as well as chemical preservation of these monuments/sites; prevention of vandalism/encroachment at
 these monuments/sites, setting up and maintenance of site, museums, environmental development of monuments/sites;
 (iii) bringing out of archaeological publications (iv) epigraphical research (v) operation of antiquarian law viz. Ancient
 Monuments and Archaeological sites and Remains Act-1958 and Rules 1959; as well as Antiquities & Art Treasures
 Act, 1972 and Rules 1976; (vi) bringing out of archaeological publications (vii) maintenance and upkeep of
 archaeological libraries.
Laying down of archaeological policy in the country, and to issue licences for conducting archaeological excavations by
 various states/research Institution and generally guide archaeological activities in the country.

 Survey of India had no basic qualification or knowledge in archaeology.

SARASVATI PROJECT
25.       The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, govern excavations in India.  The
 Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India grants licenses to various excavation agencies, both government
 and autonomous, for conducting excavations on the recommendations of the standing Committee of the Central
 Advisory Board of Archaeology (CABA).  The criteria for selecting a site for excavation are as under:
bridging of missing gaps(s) in the cultural sequence of Indian archaeology,
throwing more light on lesser known cultures.
Salvage archaeology in the event of a site being submerged by a dam or being destroyed or damaged due to absolutely
 necessary development works, natural calamities.

 Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat and formulating and implementing integrated development programmes in the area by
 creating 15 hub sites as centers of culture, tourism and good civic life.   For providing a proper orientation as well as
 implementation of the Project, the Government of India through its gazette notification S.O. 1329 (E), dated 18
th
 December 2002, New Delhi, constituted a 13 member committee namely, the Advisory Committee, for the
 Multidisciplinary Study of River Sarasvati (ACMS), under the chairmanship of the then Minister of Tourism and
 Culture.

 (MASI) No. 98 Likewise, report on Adam Excavations (1988-1992) is in press as MASI No. 99.  Some excavations are
 still ongoing and some of them are at various stages of completion.
42.       Regarding delay in writing the excavation reports, the Archaeological Survey of India informed that the delay is
 due to their nature and scope, as these are supposed to be the comprehensive research documents, containing
 information on excavated structures, stratigraphical features, supported by maps, illustrations – photo-documentation
 and line-drawings of excavated structures, potteries, artifacts, and other materials.  The report also would have to
 incorporate detailed technical and scientific reports and bibliographical references.  Since a huge body of data is
 generated in course of excavation, it takes time to organize and describe that exhaustive database on factual and
 interpretative lines.  For report writing, a team of excavators, who participated in that very excavation, is required to
 discuss, prepare research notes, and correlate the excavation findings for description in terms of time and space.  This is
 true in case of all excavations.  This has been further complicated the officers were sometime transferred before they
 could complete the reports.
43.       However, the important results of all excavations carried out by the Archaeological Survey of India are
 published in the Indian Archaeology – A review (IAR), an annual publication of the Archaeological Survey of India.

46.       The Committee is of the view that if excavation reports are not written, then all the taxpayers’ money spent on
 them goes waste.  Also, in absence of timely publication of excavation reports, the achievements of Archaeological
 Survey of India largely remain unnoticed by the public.  The Committee is extremely dissatisfied to observe that
 despite its repeated recommendations, the position in respect of writing of excavation reports has not improved much. 
 However, the Committee is hopeful that the steps now initiated by Archaeological Survey of India for clearing the
 backlog in respect of writing excavation reports would yield some positive results.  The Committee recommends that
 the Archaeological Survey of India should enforce a fixed time frame for writing excavation reports after the
 excavation work has been completed, so that the public at large is not deprived of the vital right to information.  The
 Committee also recommends that the ASI should ensure that officials engaged in a particular excavation work are not
 transferred till such time that they complete the excavations and submit their reports.

CONSERVATION/PRESERVATION OF MONUMENTS AND REGISTRATION OF ANTIQUITIES
54.       The Committee also enquired about the procedure adopted for conservation/preservation of the monuments.  The
 Committee was informed that whenever an ancient structure or an archaeological site/remain is considered be of
 national importance, a proposal to this effect is initiated by the circle office and sent to the Director General,
 Archaeological Survey of India along with its historical, archaeological and architectural importance.  On receipt of the
 approval of the Director General, Archaeological Survey of India, the proposal is forwarded to the State Government
 with detailed drawings for the counter signature of the Deputy Commissioner/Commissioner concerned.  On receipt of
 the revenue data duly counter signed, the Central Government issues a notification of its intentions to declare the
 monument as of national importance with a two months notice.  On the expiry of notice period and after considering the
 objections, if any, a final Gazette notification is issued for declaring the said monument as a monument of national
 importance.
55.       The State Governments are consulted if the proposed monument is State protected and is proposed to be taken
 over by the Archaeological Survey of India.  In all other cases, State Governments are involved only to the extent of
 preparation of relevant revenue papers required for the notification or subsequently, if land or building compensation is
 involved.
56.       The Committee was further informed that the basic guidelines for conservation have been framed with an
 objective to prolong the life of monuments without the loss of artistic and historical values.  It is important for
 archaeological values to preserve the original fabric of the monument to the extent possible.  Archaeological Survey of
 India follows a Conservation Manual which contains detailed guidelines for execution of conservation works.  The
 conservation and preservation of monuments aim at :
its preservation without disfigurement or alteration of its character;
its maintenance in a proper and attractive condition;
the complete examination of its remains and documentary evidence concerning it; and
 
the preparation of monographs, guide books and reports so that its historical and artistic interest may be perpetuated.
57.       Apart from this the monuments which had garden around them as part of their original design are taken up for
 restoration and maintenance and wherever it was not part of original layout/feature, beautification through landscaping
 is also undertaken.  However, it has been decided to compile a comprehensive conservation manual during the 10
th Five
 Year Plan period incorporating extant guidelines of Archaeological Survey of India and relevant features of
 internationally acceptable conservation guidelines and norms.
58.       The Committee is of the view that beautification and development of archaeological sites no doubt adds to the
 ambience of these sites.  However, the Committee recommends that while taking up work, the focus should be on

 Commission, Department of Expenditure, IFD etc., the matter was reconsidered in consultation with the Archaeological
 Survey of India.  It was suggested that since the nature of work for the two Missions was complementary to each other
 both the Missions should be carried out by one structural network since in both the cases, the nodal agency was going
 to be Archaeological Survey of India.  The overall project cost of Rs.400 crore also needed to be pruned drastically

 Missions it was therefore decided to reduce the Missions’ outlay to about Rs.90 crore to make it compact and viable so

 proposal has been recast into a single Mission proposal.  By merging them together, the financial outlay required for
 undertaking both the Missions has been greatly reduced and the goals are also justified.”

MONUMMENTS/SITES UNDER PROTECTION OF ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee notes that the ASI has drawn long-term programme to protect all 3663 monuments/sites of national

ORGANISATIONAL SET UP AND THE POST OF DIRECTOR GENERAL OF THE ARCHAEOLOGICAL
 SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee is not in agreement with the argument put- forth by the Ministry of Culture that the appointment of
 generalist administrator as Director General will not hamper the development of Archaeological Survey of India as a
 scientific organisation.  The Committee is shocked to note that even after the Gazette Notification of May 2002, the
 Government has not been able to fill up the post of Director General, Archaeological Survey of India as per the
 requirements of the notification and has been merely filling up the post from Indian Administrative Service on
 deputation basis.  The Committee is constrained to observe that the Government preferred to fill up the highest post of
 an apex institution requiring very high standards of technical qualification with a generalist administrator.  The
 Committee is of the view that a person who has no basic qualification or knowledge of archaeology cannot handle the
 apex responsibility of a Scientific Institution like Archaeological Survey of India.  Unless the leader of the
 Archaeological Survey of India is having the professional expertise, it is very difficult to give a lead.  This has also
 dampened the spirits of the senior officers in the feeder grade of the organization who may never get the opportunities
 to serve as senior most officer of their parent organization.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that steps should be
 taken to fill up the post of Director General, Archaeological Survey of India as per the requirements of the Notification
 of May 2002, at the earliest.
ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA AS A SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNICAL DEPARTMENT
The Committee is constrained to note that even after a lapse of fifteen years from the date of issue of the notification in
 this regard no concrete action was taken by Ministry of Culture and Archaeological Survey of India for developing
 Archaeological Survey of India as a Scientific and Technical Department, which amply indicates the administrative
 apathy towards the whole issue.  The Committee regrets that no internal exercise was undertaken by Ministry of
 Culture and Archaeological Survey of India during the last fifteen years for availing the benefits and privileges which
 could be extended to the Archaeological Survey of India as a Science and Technology department.  The Committee
 observes that there has been deviation in the working of Archaeological Survey of India and that it has failed in terms
 of developing Archaeological Survey of India not merely as an administrative body but also as a spearhead for
 consolidating the scientific discipline of archaeology in the country.  The Committee is of the view that the
 Archaeological Survey of India needs to reinvent itself, not merely as an administrative wing of the Government, but as
 an agency for protecting and safeguarding our national heritage, which involves a lot of scientific and technical work. 
 Unless the Archaeological Survey of India converts itself fully into a scientific and technical organization, the basic
 role and function of the organisation will be defeated.   The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture and
 Archaeological Survey of India should, without any further loss of time, take necessary follow-up action on the
 recommendations of the Committee chaired by Director General, Archaeological Survey of India so as to avail the
 benefits which accrue to a Science and Technology department.  The Committee also recommends that, if required, the
 Ministry of Culture should also take necessary legislative action to make Archaeological Survey of India Science and
 Technology department in the true sense.

 replies submitted to the Committee by the Department of Culture.  On the one hand, the Ministry of Culture has stated
 that the former Minister of Tourism and Culture was not the Chairman of the Sarasvati Heritage Project, while, on the
 other hand, the Ministry has stated that prior to the preparation of the project report, the Government had constituted an
 Advisory Committee with the then Minister of Tourism and Culture as Chairman and that this Committee had
 recommended the Saraswati Heritage Project.  The Committee further notes that the Ministry is not clear as to which
 research agency/scientific survey actually pointed out that the dry beds of River Ghaggar and River Chautang (River
 Drisadvati) are the bed of River Sarasvati.  The Committee understands that existence of River Sarasvati is purely a
 mythological one and a scientific institution like Archaeological Survey of India has not correctly proceeded in the

The Committee notes with concern that there are large-scale vacancies in various categories in the ASI, which has been

NON-WRITING/PUBLICATION OF EXCAVATION REPORTS
The Committee is of the view that if excavation reports are not written, then all the taxpayers’ money spent on them
 goes waste.  Also, in absence of timely publication of excavation reports, the achievements of Archaeological Survey of
 India largely remain unnoticed by the public.  The Committee is extremely dissatisfied to observe that despite its
 repeated recommendations, the position in respect of writing of excavation reports has not improved much.  However,
 the Committee is hopeful that the steps now initiated by Archaeological Survey of India for clearing the backlog in
 respect of writing excavation reports would yield some positive results.  The Committee recommends that the
 Archaeological Survey of India should enforce a fixed time frame for writing excavation reports after the excavation
 work has been completed, so that the public at large is not deprived of the vital right to information.  The Committee
 also recommends that the ASI should ensure that officials engaged in a particular excavation work are not transferred
 till such time that they complete the excavations and submit their reports.
ENCROACHMENT AND SECURITY OF MONUMENTS/SITES
The Committee is concerned about the illegal encroachment of monuments/archaeological sites under the protection of
 Archaeological Survey of India.  In this context, the Committee would like to reiterate the recommendation made in its
 85
th Report on Demands for Grants 2005-06 of Ministry of Culture which is as under:
"The Committee expresses its anxiety over the incidents of encroachment upon the land of Centrally Protected
 Monuments.  The Committee is more concerned about the inability of Archeological Survey of India to get back the
 land from encroachers.  Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that a complete assessment should be made
 regarding encroachment of monuments/sites under the protection of Archaeological Survey of India all over the
 country.  Prompt action ought be taken against the encroachers with the help of State Governments/Local
 Administrations and the matter should be pursued at the highest level.  The Committee also recommends that adequate
 budgetary provisions should be made for security arrangements and protection of monuments, as this is the most crucial
 aspect of preserving our cultural heritage and wherever possible modern gadgets like, electronic surveillance cameras
 should be installed in the monuments.  The Committee feels that security is a sovereign function.  Hence, it is the
 responsibility of Central Government to get the monuments and other important assets protected.  In view of this, the
 Committee is of the opinion that the Union Home Ministry should pay the bills towards the expenses incurred for
 paying the Central Security Agencies under this head.  Accordingly, the Ministry of Culture should pursue the matter at
 the highest level." 
CONSERVATION/PRESERVATION OF MONUMENTS AND REGISTRATION OF ANTIQUITIES
The Committee is of the view that beautification and development of archaeological sites no doubt adds to the ambience
 of these sites.  However, the Committee recommends that while taking up work, the focus should be on actual

 conservation/preservation work undertaken by the Archaeological Survey of India.  The Committee also recommends
 that more amount should be spent on conservation/preservation of the sites in comparison to site
 development/beautification etc. 
The Committee notes the response of the Archaeological Survey of India to the observations made by the Committee in
 its 85
th Report on Demands for Grants 2005-06 of Ministry of Culture.  The Committee hopes that with the existing
 staff and expertise, Archaeological Survey of India would be able to successfully execute the National Mission for

The Committee observes that the Ministry of Culture has decided to involve private agencies in handling the National
 Mission of Antiquities.  The Committee recommends that adequate care should be taken while finalizing such kind of
 deal so that the expenditure to be incurred on the National Mission of Antiquities is spent in the best interest of the
 nation and the valuable information about Indian Antiquities and Monuments are not handed over to foreign hands.

ANALYSIS OF THE TENTH PLAN PROVISIONS AND ANNUAL                                    PLAN 2005-06
(Recommendation at Para 20) 
 
5.         The Committee regrets to note that BE Plan Provision of Rs.7912 crore of Department of Road Transport and
 Highways was brought down to Rs.6766 crore on account of slow implementation of Externally Aided Projects by
 NHAI and the Department.  Further, there was delay in finalization of the loans and obtaining approvals for the
 procurement for the externally aided component of the Corridor Project of NHDP (Phase-II) being financed by the
 Asian Development Bank (ADB).  Also, there was delay in award of works to the contractors and consultants for
 development of NH-34 in West Bengal.  These instances clearly bring out that on the one hand, the Department of
 Road Transport and Highways emphasizes that funds for development and maintenance of National Highways are
 inadequate while, on the other hand, the Department is not able to utilise the higher allocation made to it at BE stage.  
 The Department has failed to make optimal utilization of the funds at its disposal. The reasons for shortfall mentioned
 are delay in land acquisition, poor performance of the contractors, law and order problem etc. are very general in nature
 and are repeated every year. As a result of these, the budgetary allocations of the Department were reduced at RE
 stage.  The Committee is of the view that there is a lack of monitoring system in the Department of Road Transport and
 Highways.  The lack of a proper monitoring system in the Department is exemplified by the delay and non-completion
 of the construction of flyover at Murthal in Haryana and the failure of the Department of Road Transport and Highways
 in verifying the credentials of the contractors who had submitted forged bank guarantees.  The Committee observes that
 the budget allocations of the Department of Road Transport and Highways have been substantially increased during
 2005-06. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should devise
 strategies, whereby they are able to fully utilize the funds at their disposal.  They should also evolve some mechanism
 to identify bottlenecks causing delays and work towards resolving all such hindrances in coordination with all the
 concerned agencies.  This would also help them to avoid time overrun and consequential cost overrun of the projects to
 be executed by them.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
 
6.         The main reason for non-utilization of the approved funds of 2004-05 was non-execution of loan agreements
 with Asian Development Bank (ADB) and World Bank for Projects under NHDP-Phase-II due to procedural delay like
 clearance from ADB / World Bank, high tender rates, delay in signing loan agreement, etc.  However, most of the
 problems have now been resolved.

 contained in its Eighty Sixth Report on Demands for Grants (2005-06) (Demand No. 85) of the Department of

th April, 2005.
2.         Action Taken Replies have been received from the Government on 29th August, 2005 in respect of all the
 observations/recommendations contained in the Report.  These have been categorized as follows:-
(i)         Recommendations/observations that have been accepted by the Government:

3.         The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which have been categorized as
 interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the earliest.
4.         On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each item of the action
 taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry.  The recommendations of the Committee contained in the Eighty Sixth 
 Report, action taken thereon by the Government and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of
 action taken have been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
ANALYSIS OF ANNUAL PLAN 2005-06
(Recommendation at Para No. 10&11)
 
5.The Committee expresses its concern over the failure of Department of Shipping to spend the approved outlay. 
 During the year 2004-05, out of the budgeted amount of Rs.2419.66 crore the Department could spent only Rs.1400.99
 crore which clearly indicates the poor fiscal management in the Department of Shipping.  The Committee observes that
 even while revising allocations, little consideration has been paid to the actual expenditure incurred in the past.  This
 shows that budgetary and revised estimates have always been made without taking into account the actual requirements
 as experienced in the previous years.
 6.The Committee feels that Department of Shipping has not evolved effective system or planning to systematically
 anticipate, assess and project its actual requirements of funds otherwise the investments could have yielded
 commensurate returns.  The Committee recommends that in future, the Department of Shipping should be transparent
 and realistic while making projections of required funds so that resources may not remain unused and are allocated
 more judiciously.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
Ports Wing
7.         The Annual Plan outlay during the year 2004-05 for the Port Sector was Rs.1066.95 crores. Actual expenditure
 was Rs.341.62 crores (Provisional).
8.         The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee are accepted and have been brought to the notice of Chairmen
 of Major Ports and heads of other organizations. Allocations for various projects under the Annual Plan are made after
 carrying out an assessment of the requirements on year to year basis. The Annual Plan proposals are formulated about
 five to six months in advance before the commencement of the Annual Plan period after factoring in the anticipated
 expenditure during the current year and the assessed requirements in the ensuing Annual Plan year for on-going
 projects and taking into account the assessed requirement of funds for the new projects to be taken up during the
 ensuing Annual Plan year. Requirements of funds at the Revised Estimates stage is projected after carrying out a review
 of the progress in the expenditure during the year till that time and after taking into account the anticipated expenditure
 during the remaining part of the year. This does not necessarily follow a uniform or standard pattern every year.
 
9.         In view of the time lag between the formulation process for Annual Plan and the implementation period, there is
 generally mismatch between the allocations and the actual expenditure. The ports were advised that there should be
 realistic approach while proposing the Annual Plan outlay for 2005-06 and that only token provision may be kept for
 projects for which administrative approval was yet to be accorded by the Competent Authority. The recommendations
 of the Committee will be kept in view while finalizing the allocation for Annual Plans in future also.
 
Shipping Wing
 
10.       The Budgetary Support to the extent of Rs. 152.50 crore was provided in BE 2004-05 for the Shipping Sector.
 This was reduced to Rs. 132.12 crore at RE 2004-05 stage. The actual expenditure was Rs. 119.49 crore.
 
11.       The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee are accepted and have been brought to the notice of all
 concerned offices/PSUs under the Shipping Wing. Allocations for various projects under the Annual Plan are made
 after carrying out an assessment of the requirements on year to year basis. The Annual Plan proposals are formulated
 about five to six months in advance before the commencement of the annual Plan period after factoring in the
 anticipated expenditure during the current year and the assessed requirements in the ensuing Annual Plan year for on-
going projects and taking into account the assessed requirement of funds for the new projects to be taken up during the

 of the progress in the expenditure during the year till that time and after taking into account the anticipated expenditure

PORT SECTOR
(Recommendation at Para No. 16)
14.       The Committee is unhappy with the poor performance of Department of Shipping with regard to under
 utilization of approved outlays over the years for the port sector.  During the Financial year 2004-05, an outlay of
 Rs.1066.55 crore was allocated for the port sector but the ports could utilize only Rs.440.51 crore. The Committee is
 dismayed by this repeated failure of Department of Shipping and is surprised as to why the Ministry asks for so much
 of allocation if it is not in position to spend the approved outlay. The Committee desires that the Department of
 Shipping should take all corrective measures based upon actual requirements for maximum utilization of budgeted
 amount during 2005-06.  In this regard, the Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation contained in 81
st report of
 Demands for Grants (2004-05) of Ministry of Shipping which reads as under:-
"The Committee fails to understand as to how the physical targets will be achieved with this low utilization pattern.  In
 fact, the Committee feels that this raises doubts about the mismatch in the projections for physical and financial
 targets.  The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Shipping has full responsibility to ensure proper utilization
 of the approved outlay.  The Committee feels that strict monitoring is crucial for timely completion of any project. 
 Therefore, the Committee recommends that the monitoring agency should play rather proactive role and do away with
 the procedural hurdles for timely completion of the projects so that the budgeted allocation is utilized optimally.  The
 Committee also recommends the Ministry to keep informed about the progress in the matter."
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
15.       The Annual Plan outlay during the year 2004-05 for the Port Sector was Rs.1066.95 crores. Actual expenditure
 was Rs.341.62 crores (Provisional).
 
16.       The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee are accepted and have been brought to the notice of Chairmen
 of Major Ports and heads of other organizations. The Department has impressed upon the Port Chairmen etc., the
 imperative for formulation of Plan schemes based on a critical review of requirements and close monitoring of the pace
 of expenditure. They have been advised to strengthen the institutional mechanisms and ensure concerted and focused
 participation from top down to ensure timely utilization of plan funds and also to facilitate a meaningful discussion on
 plan expenditure in the Board meetings. Secretary (Shipping) held two meetings during 2004-05 specially to review the
 pace of expenditure. Close monitoring continues to be carried out on utilization of the plan funds during 2005-06 and
 will continue to be carried out with a view to ensure optimal utilization of funds.

17.       The Committee notes the reply and expects that the mechanism evolved by the Department of Shipping remains
 fool-proof and problems of fiscal management would not be encountered in future.
CAPACITY AND TRAFFIC IN MAJOR PORT
(Recommendation at Para No. 26 & 27
18.The Committee expresses its appreciation for achievement of the capacity of major ports which has either exceeded
 the target or likely to achieve target fixed for cargo handling of all commodities except container.  The containerization
 is the emerging global trend in the mode of cargo trade in which the country is lagging behind which is a matter of
 concern.
           
19.The Committee feels that a proper environment with transparent procedures and decision making process can give
 boost to private sector participation in the port sector.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department of
 Shipping to review the existing guidelines on Private Sector Participation in the port sector with emphasis on

REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT

20.       The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee are accepted. Department of Shipping is in the process of
 revising the existing guidelines on private sector participation in major ports with a view to making them investor

21.     The Committee notes the reply furnished by the Ministry.
TONNAGE TAX
(Recommendation at Para 31)
22.The Committee notes that the Government has since introduced the tonnage tax regime to the dredgers also as per its
 recommendation.  The Committee feels that  introduction of tonnage tax  in lieu of corporate tax  will not only facilitate
 investment in Shipping Sector but also provide a level playing field to the Indian Shipping Industry vis-à-vis its foreign 
 counterparts and the Indian Shipping companies will be able to acquire more tonnage.  Howeveer, the Committee is
  unable  to comprehend the reasons for excluding  the  vessels registered under the Indian Vessels Act, 1917 and Indian
 Coastal Vessel Act 1838.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the matter for  extending the benefit of tonnage
 tax to vessels registered under Indian Vessels Act, 1917 and Indian Coastal Vessels Act 1838 may be pursued further
 with the Ministry of Finance as this also vitally linked to the viability of the Inland Water Transport sector
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
23.       The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech of 2005-06 have announced that the ‘Dredgers’ would also come
 under tonnage tax regime. However, The vessels registered under Inland Vessels Act 1917 and Coastal Vessels Act,
 1838 are left out and tonnage tax benefit has not been extended  to the vessels covered under these two Act.
24.       This Ministry had already taken up the matter with Ministry of Finance for inclusion of vessels registered under
 Indian Vessel Act and Coasting Vessel Act, which were enjoying the benefits of Section 33 AC but now lost that
 benefits. Simultaneously these have been kept out of tonnage tax benefits also.   As directed by the Committee,
 Ministry of Finance was requested to consider the matter and include the vessels under the above Acts in the tonnage
 tax regime.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
25.    The Committee suggests the Department of  Shipping to pursue the matter persistently with the Department of
 Finance .
SETHUSAMUDRAM SHIP CHANNEL PROJECT
(Recommendation at Para 36)
 26.      The Committee notes the Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project is of great economic and strategic importance
 which will connect the Gulf of Mannar to Bay of Bengal so that the ship moving between East and West coast of India
 could have a continuous navigable sea route within their own territorial waters and the proposed channel save upto 424
 nautical miles of travel and about 30 hours of sailing time for ships.  The Committee notes with satisfaction that
 Ministry of Environment & Forests has also given environmental clearance to the project and a special purpose vehicle
 has been incorporated to raise finance to create and operate navigable channel.  The Committee expects that the project
 once completed will serve the strategic and national security interests besides spuring the overall economic
 development of coastal districts of southern states.  The Committee however, recommends that while taking up the
 implementation of the project, the Department of Shipping must give due attention to the likely effect of natural
 calamities particularly one like as Tsunami which hit southern states during December 2004 and safety measures may
 be incorporated accordingly.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
27.       The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee are accepted.The Government sanction for implementing
 Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project at a cost of Rs.2427.40 crores has been issued on 1
st June, 2005. The animation
 models of the Tsunami of 26th December, 2004 available with the Tuticorin Port Trust indicates that the project area
 was the least affected on the east coast by the Tsunami. Hydrodynamic modeling studies recently carried out have
 confirmed the earlier findings that increase in magnitude of the current in the post-channel era will be only along the
 channel in Adam’s Bridge with no change in current status alongside the channel. The issues relating to Tsunami and
 impact of cyclonic storms over the channel were also duly examined by the Ministry of Environment & Forests before
 according environmental clearance. However, during the execution phase, suggestions of the experts will be duly taken
 into consideration by the project authorities to ensure that the impact of natural calamities on the channel is
 insignificant. An Environmental Monitoring Committee comprising experts/officials has been set up by the
 Government for monitoring of various environmental issues connected with the implementation of the project which
 will meet at least once a month and submit its report to the Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport & Highways.

FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
28.The Committee notes with appreciation the initiatives taken by the Government in the matter.
CRUISE SHIPPING
(Recommendation at Para 40)
 
29.       The Committee is of the view that sea travel is becoming increasingly popular and there is enormous potential
 for its growth and expansion in India. The Committee notes that six major ports- Mumbai, Mormugao, New Mangalore,
 Kochi, Tuticorin and Chennai have been identified for the development of infrastructure and other facilities with a view
 to make India an attractive cruise destination. The Committee notes that a High Power Steering Group has been set up
 with a view to catalyze the growth and development of cruise shipping and to remove bottlenecks and a policy is being
 formulated in this regard. The Committee hopes that the group will submit its report expeditiously and the policy is
 framed at the earliest so that the benefit of opportunity available to cruise tourism sector is exploited. The Committee
 recommends that pending finalization of policy, the Department of Shipping must take steps to attract investments from
 private sector with a view to create infrastructure and other facilities for development of cruise shipping especially in
 ports on the Eastern parts of  the country including Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshdweep Islands having great potential
 in that area.  
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
30.       The suggestions/recommendations of the Committee have been noted for taking necessary action.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
  31.    The Committee may be apprised of the action taken by the Department of Shipping in this regard.
 
CALCUTTA  DOCK LABOUR BOARD
(Recommendation at Para 49-51)
 
32.       The Committee is distressed to note that the employees of the Calcutta Dock Labour Board are not being treated
 as Government employees so far as payment of pension and pensionary benefits are concerned, though, the Calcutta
 Dock Labour Board, a body corporate, was constituted in terms of section 5(A) of the Dock Workers (Regulation of
 Employment) Act, 1948 in September 1952.  The Committee expresses its concern that inspite of specific provisions
 under the Act, the rules and regulations concerning pension for employees of Calcutta Dock Labour Board have not
 been approved by Department of Expenditure and the employees of Calcutta Dock Labour Board are being made
 victims under the cover that Calcutta Dock Labour Board constitutes an autonomous body and therefore, denied of the
 benefits for long.
 
33.       The Committee is of the firm opinion that liabilities on account of payment of arrears of pensions and
 pensionary dues of Calcutta Dock Labour Board entirely lies on the Government and the Government cannot be
 absolved of its liability and withhold pension and post retirement benefits to the employees of Calcutta Dock Labour
 Board on one pretext or other.  The Committee, strongly recommends, the Department of Shipping to vigorously pursue
 the matter with Ministry of Finance for release of enhanced grant to Calcutta Dock Labour Board for meeting its
 pensionary liabilities and implement comprehensive restructuring of Calcutta Dock Labour Board for introduction of
 Voluntary Retirement Scheme.
 
34.       The Committee is of the view that problem for payment of pension and pensionary dues can be resolved once
 and for all, if the Government approves self-sustaining proposal for Calcutta Dock Labour Board's pensioners with
 provisions for an initial corpus and an appropriate policy and methodology for payment of pension worked out for the
 future.  The Committee, therefore reiterates, that the Government should build a corpus of pension fund for discharging
 the future pensionary liabilities of the Board, as the bulk of its employees will retire in another two years.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
35.       The proposal for release of enhanced grant of Rs.59.59 crores to Calcutta Dock Labour Board to meet its
 pensionery liabilities on account of revision of pensionery benefits as per wage settlement and for liberalization of post
 retirement benefits to pensioners who retired before 1.1.1998 was taken up with Ministry of Finance, who have not
 accepted the proposal.

36.       On the advise of the Department of Shipping, Calcutta Dock Labour Board has submitted a self-sustaining
 proposal seeking one time tax free grant of Rs.537.41 crores from Government of India for payment of unpaid arrears
 of Rs.80.37 crores to CDLB pensioners and workers/employees and Rs.457.04 crores for building a corpus of Pension
 Fund, out of which the future pensionary liabilities of the Board can be discharged. This is an alternative to the earlier
 proposal for release of enhanced grant of Rs.59.59 crores which has not been accepted by the Ministry of Finance. The
 proposal has been circulated to the Appraising Agencies for their views/comments before it is placed before the
 Competent Authority for approval.

37.       The Committee is constrained to note that till date Government have not decided to settle the retirement dues of
 the employees of CDLB.  Regarding introduction of Voluntary Retirements Scheme, the Committee is of the view that
 the Department of Shipping should strongly pursue the matter with the Cabinet and in the meanwhile, the advice of the
 Ministry of Law and Justice may be sought to resolve the issue. 
MISAPPROPRIATION OF SEAMEN’S PROVIDENT FUND
(Recommendation at Para 55)
38.       The Committee is deeply concerned that the shortage to the tune of Rs. 92.78 crore in Seamen’s Provident Fund,
 which lost due to security scam, has not yet been recouped by the Department of Shipping. The Committee is unable to
 comprehend the reasons for delay in recouping the fund, which is entirely managed by the Government and feels that
 any further delay may cause adverse impact in protection of interests of the seamen’s whose life long savings stands
 jeopardized in the scam. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department of Shipping to approach the Ministry
 of Finance for grants-in-aid to recoup the shortage in the Seamen’s Provident Fund.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
39.       Government is very much concerned about protection of the interests of seafarers. The Cabinet Note is being
 finalized in this regard and the advice of Ministry of Law & Justice has been sought. After the advice of Ministry of
 Law & Justice is received, a Cabinet Note will be finalized and sent to Cabinet for consideration.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
40.       The Committee is perturbed to note that previously also the Department of Shipping has submitted that the
 Cabinet Note is under finalization and no progress seems to be made in this context thereafter.  The Committee has not
 been apprised of the status of its recommendation about approaching the Ministry of Finance for grants-in-aid to recoup
 the shortage in the Seamen's Provident Fund.
 
MISAPPROPRIATION OF SEAMEN’S PROVIDENT FUND
(Recommendation at Para 56)
 
 41.      The Committee further recommends that in order to ensure that such happenings are not repeated in future,
 sufficient legislative and administrative safeguards have to be built in the system. At the same time, those responsible
 for such scam should not be spared and suitable action including criminal action ought to be taken against them so that
 such actions provide deterrence to other as well. The Committee would like to be apprised of the action in this regard.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
42.        In order to prevent such happenings in future the following measures have been taken: -
 
(i)         Resolution of 28.11.1996, authorizing the commissioner as a sole authority to do the investment has been
 rescinded.
(ii)        A reputed company (Chartered Accountants) has been appointed as Internal Auditors who submit quarterly
 report which is placed before the Board in its subsequent meetings.
(iii)       All physical securities required to be converted into demat form have been converted.  State Bank of Indore has
 been appointed as Depository Participants for the purpose.

58.       The Committee notes with distress that the matter for disinvestments of Central Inland Water Transport

 gravely concern by the fact that inspite of repeated recommendation in the past the Government has not yet been able to
 come out with a complete blueprint for making full use of the existing assets of the company in ensuring productive
 potential by exploring all possibilities like merger with similar entities and integration with Inland Water Transport.
 The Committee is firmly of the view that the future of Inland Water Transport operations including that of Central
 Water Transport Corporation Ltd.  holds immense possibilities for establishing a well-defined multimodal
 transportation network in the country and therefore recommends the Department of Shipping to take steps to improve
 the performance of the Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. besides impressing upon the Ministry of

61.       The Committee is constrained to note that Inland Water Transport has been the most neglected sector and has
 not been developed with desired pace inspite of its economic potential and merely accounts for 0.15% of cargo
 movement in the country.  The Committee observes that though measures to boost the growth of cargo traffic have been
 put in place and department is committed to raise the share of Inland Water Transport to 2% over the next 8-20 years. 
 The Committee however, notes that with a view to compete with the other developed modes of transport, the
 Department of Shipping is working on declaration and development of three more waterways as National Waterways
 and a task force to monitor the progress of Inland Water Transport projects has also been formed.  The Committee,
 recommends the Department of Shipping to exploit the full potential of this efficient mode of transport, besides,
 addressing the issues of development of adequate infrastructure facilities namely fairways, terminal and navigational
 aids on the existing three NWs.

 PLAN AND ANALYSIS OF THE ANNUAL PLAN 2005-2006

(Recommendation at Para No.9)
5.
The Committee notes that the budgetary allocation has always been less than the actual requirement and to adjust the shortfall, the allocation has to be subsequently increased.  The Committee is unable to comprehend the
reasons for keeping lower outlays when the actual requirement is far higher.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that every effort should be taken to make realistic estimation of allocation in subsequent plans keeping
in view all the anticipated demand for development of the tourism sector as a whole.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
6.         The Ministry of Tourism has always projected its budgetary requirements based on the actual needs and proposed for revision at the time of formulation of Revised Estimates, if any additional requirement is felt
necessary.  However, the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance are the final authorities for the allocations of funds in the Annual Plans of the Ministry and they have allocated less Budgetary support than the
actual requirements and projected plans.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
7.The Committee is aware of the fact that the Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission are the final authorities for the allocation of funds in the Annual Plans of the Ministry.  However, the Committee recommends
that the attention of the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance may be invited to the observations made by Committee for  allocation of Budgetary support as per actual requirement and projected plans.  Their
response may be submitted to the Committee for its consideration.
(Recommendation at Para No.13)
 
8.         
The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism has been allocated a higher amount to the tune of Rs.786.00 crore in the B.E. 2005-06 which is almost 57 per cent over and above the approved outlay for the year
2004-05.  However, the Committee expresses its concern over the under utilisations of funds by the Ministry during the year 2004-05 and notes that the Ministry could spend only 79 per cent of the allocation i.e. Rs.395.1
crore out of the budgeted allocation of Rs.500 crore upto February 2005.  The Committee also notes that larger part of the budgeted amount was spent at the fag end of the financial year, especially, in the months of
February and March, which is much against the financial norms.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the programmes and policies should be implemented in a manner, which ensures regular infusion of
funds in various projects/schemes uniformly in all quarters of the financial year.  The Committee expects that the Ministry of Tourism will be in a better position to suitably revise the plan outlays in future. 
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
9.      The Ministry of Tourism during the year 2004-05 has utilized its 92.30% out of the total budgetary allocation of Rs.503.50 crore.  The Ministry of Tourism has spent Rs.347.95 crore i.e. 69.11% of its total budget
by 31.12.2004.  The reasons for the underutilization during the year 2004-05 were due to late restoration of the cut of Rs.100 crore in B.E. 2004-05 of the Ministry of Tourism by the Ministry of Finance, and non-
approval of re-appropriation proposals.  However, the suggestions of the Committee will be kept in view while formulating its future Annual Plans.

34.       The Committee notes that during the year 2003, around 6 million Indians have visited abroad against a total incoming flow of 2.73 million foreign tourists, and more and more countries are queuing up to attract the

international market.  The Committee feels that a relative change in the marketing strategy is required for tapping the domestic and international tourism markets and recommends that special emphasis must be laid for
accessing the market by consolidation of efforts to arrest the increasing trend of outbound tourists.

The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the observations/
 recommendations as contained in its           Eighty-eighth Report on Demands for Grants (2005-2006) (Demand No. 9) of
 Ministry of Civil Aviation, which was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 29
th April, 2005.
 
 2.         Action Taken Replies have been received from the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 30
th September, 2005 in respect of
 all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report, which have been categorised as follows: -
 
(i)         Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry:
Para Nos. 9, 42, 55, 108, 135 and 136                                                    Total- 6
(ii)        Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Ministry’s replies:
Para Nos. 22, 86, 90, 109 and 138                                                           Total- 5
(iii)       Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not been accepted by the

 Committee:
